EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

================================================================  
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Strategy: 2-stage least-squares Difference-in-Differences / Event-Study that instruments the immigrant inflow into (region r × year t) with an exogenous “shift–share” (a.k.a. Bartik) measure based on (i) the sudden national-level inflow of refugees/Aussiedler from 1989-1995 (the “shift”) and (ii) each region’s immigrant‐network/dispersal quota in 1988 (the “share”).  

Why appropriate:  
• Massive geopolitical shock generates plausibly exogenous time-series “shift”.  
• Pre-1990 spatial settlement patterns + legally mandated dispersal rules generate cross-sectional “shares” predetermined to the shock.  
• Combining the two gives quasi-random variation in the immigrant share of every region over time.  
• Using region × skill-cell (education × experience) panels allows us to replicate both “area” and “skill” estimands in one unified framework while controlling for national skill-group trends and region-specific shocks.  
• A DID/Event-study specification (with region and year fixed effects) isolates within-region changes before vs. after the shock, so that remaining identifying variation is the interaction of the shock with pre-determined shares.  

Econometrically:  

1st stage:  ImmShare_{r,t} = π · PredictedInflow_{r,t} + Region_FE + Year_FE + ε  
2nd stage:  Y_{r,s,t} = β · Ŝ ImmShare_{r,t} + γ X_{r,s,t} + Region×Skill_FE + Year×Skill_FE + error  

Y = log wage or employment of natives in region r, skill cell s, year t.  
β identifies the causal effect of an immigrant on native outcomes for the average skill cell in the region (area × skill hybrid). Event-study bins event time (t–1989) to trace pre-trends.  

================================================================  
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable  
T_{r,t} = actual immigrant share (# immigrants / total employment) in region r and year t, instrumented by PredictedInflow_{r,t}.  

Control group  
Regions whose pre-1989 network/dispersal share was small. Counterfactual path comes from their outcomes over the same years, plus all regions in pre-period (1985-1988).  

Treatment timing  
Event date = 1990 (start of large inflow). Pre-period 1985-1989; post-period 1990-2000 (and up to 2008 for persistence).  

No RDD running variable; the design is IV-DID.  

================================================================  
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Relevance: Regions that hosted more co-ethnics or were allocated more immigrants ex-ante indeed receive larger post-1990 immigrant inflows. Highly plausible; historically documented.  

A2. Exogeneity (exclusion): Conditional on fixed effects and controls, pre-1989 networks/quotas affect native wages/employment only through actual immigrant inflow, not through other channels (e.g., differential local trends). Reasonable because networks were formed 40+ years earlier and quotas depend on population & tax revenue, not on 1990s labor-market forecasts.  

A3. Parallel trends / No differential pre-trends: In absence of the immigration shock, high-share and low-share regions would have evolved similarly. Can be inspected with event-study coefficients t < 0.  

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): Immigration into one region does not directly affect outcomes in other regions once we control for national-year shocks. Spatial spillovers are limited because of administrative labor-market boundaries; robustness will re-aggregate to larger spatial units.  

A5. Linear aggregation: Aggregating individual data to region × skill cells does not introduce composition bias because we keep the full universe and weight cells by employment.  

================================================================  
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & REMEDIES  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Endogenous economic migration of natives across regions.  
   – Remedy: Use individual-level panel to restrict to stayers (natives observed in same region 2 yrs pre- & post-event). Show results robust to weighting by initial native population.  

T2. Local demand shocks correlated with network size (e.g., booming Ruhrgebiet had both jobs and early immigrant communities).  
   – Remedy: include region-specific linear trends, region × industry employment shares as controls, and alternative instrument based on mandatory dispersal key (excluding network component).  

T3. Violation of exclusion if quotas affect fiscal transfers or asylum-service employment.  
   – Remedy: Drop public-sector wages from outcome; instrument only with ex-USSR/Aussiedler networks while studying Yugoslav inflow (and vice-versa) so that network ethnicity ≠ local public spending.  

================================================================  
5. R CODE OUTLINE (simplified)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# --- 0. Packages ------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)     # fast high-dimensional FE with IV
library(did)        # event-study pre-trend plots
# ---------------------------------------------------------------

# --- 1. Load and merge -----------------------------------------
ieb <- fread("IEB_panel_1985_2008.csv")      # individual-level

# --- 2. Construct variables ------------------------------------
# Education (4 groups) & Experience (5-yr bands)
ieb[, exp_band := pmin(40, as.integer(experience/5)*5)]
ieb[, skill_cell := paste(education, exp_band, sep="_")]

# Collapse to region-skill-year
agg <- ieb[, .(
  natives     = sum(native == 1),
  imm         = sum(native == 0),
  wage_nat    = weighted.mean(wage[native==1], w = employment_days[native==1]),
  emp_nat     = sum(employed[native==1])
), by = .(region, skill_cell, year)]

# Immigrant share in region-year (all skills)
region_tot <- agg[, .(imm_tot = sum(imm), natives_tot = sum(natives)), by = .(region, year)]
region_tot[, imm_share := imm_tot / (imm_tot + natives_tot)]
agg <- merge(agg, region_tot[,.(region,year,imm_share)], by=c("region","year"))

# --- 3. Build Bartik instrument -------------------------------
# (a) Pre-1989 refugee origin shares
pre_netw <- ieb[year==1988 & native==0,
                .N, by=.(region, origin)]
pre_netw[, share := N/sum(N), by=region]

# (b) National inflow by origin × year
nat_inflow <- fread("national_inflow_origin_year.csv") # 1989-2000
setnames(nat_inflow, "inflow", "shift")

# (c) Predicted inflow
pred <- merge(pre_netw, nat_inflow, by="origin", allow.cartesian=TRUE)
pred[, pred_inflow := share * shift]
pred <- pred[, .(predicted = sum(pred_inflow)), by=.(region, year)]

agg <- merge(agg, pred, by=c("region","year"))

# --- 4. Main 2SLS specification -------------------------------
fe_formula <- "log(wage_nat) ~ 1 | region + year + skill_cell:year + region:skill_cell"
iv_formula <- feols(as.formula(paste(fe_formula, "| (imm_share ~ predicted)")), data=agg, cluster = "region")

summary(iv_formula)

# --- 5. Event-study pre-trend -------------------------------
agg[, event_time := year - 1989]
agg <- agg[event_time >= -5 & event_time <= 10]  # window

iv_es <- feols(log(wage_nat) ~ i(event_time, imm_share, ref=-1) | region + skill_cell + year,
               iv = ~ i(event_time, predicted, ref=-1), data=agg, cluster="region")
iplot(iv_es)

# --- 6. Robustness: alternative instrument -------------------
# Instrument based only on dispersal quota
# (assume quota_pred variable already merged)
iv_alt <- feols(log(wage_nat) ~ 1 | region + year + skill_cell:year + region:skill_cell | 
                  (imm_share ~ quota_pred), data=agg, cluster="region")
summary(iv_alt)
```

================================================================  
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Prediction:  
• Area-level (β_area): Small negative or zero effect on average native wages (≈ –0.1 % per 1 pp immigrant share) in line with Card-type findings, because firm expansion and complementarities offset competition.  
• Skill-cell within-area (our β above): Larger negative impact (≈ –0.4 % to –0.6 % per 1 pp) for directly competing natives, revealing downgrading within skill cells.  
• Employment effects likely negligible for high-skill natives, mildly negative for low-skill/young.  

Magnitude prior comes from German literature (Dustmann et al. 2017; Brücker et al. 2001).  

================================================================  
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (IV design)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: Relevance (first-stage F > 10) ............................... 1  
C2: Exclusion (networks/quotas affect Y only via inflow) ........ 0.8  
C3: Parallel pre-trends (event-study flat pre-1990) ............. 0.8  
C4: No selective native migration (checked with stayers) ........ 0.7  
C5: SUTVA / limited spillovers (tested with spatial buffers) .... 0.7  

Average ≈ 0.8 ⇒ Design reasonably strong but not bullet-proof.
